h1: Brewing an amber ale at home with crystal malt
title: Brewing an Amber Ale With Crystal Malt | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew an amber ale at home using crystal malt for colour, caramel and body, without making it sweet or cloying. A 20 litre recipe included.
teaser: Crystal malt makes an amber ale. Too much of it ruins one. Here is how to use it well.
standfirst: An amber ale sits between a pale ale and a brown ale: copper coloured, caramel flavoured and balanced by hops. Crystal malt does most of that work. Using it well is the whole lesson of this beer.
sections: An amber ale is a copper to reddish brown ale, usually around 4.5% to 6% ABV. It has a caramel and toffee malt backbone with some toast, balanced by moderate to fairly firm hop bitterness. American versions often have a clear citrus or pine hop aroma. The finish should be fairly dry, not sugary. Our guide to amber and red ales covers the different versions, from Irish red to American amber.

Crystal malt, also called caramel malt, is made by stewing wet, germinated barley so the starches convert to sugar inside the husk, then drying or roasting it. The sugars caramelise. The result adds colour, caramel and toffee flavours, some body and a little residual sweetness.

Crystal malts come in a range of colours. Light ones, around 20 to 60 EBC, add honey and light caramel. Medium ones, around 100 to 150 EBC, add toffee and darker caramel. Dark ones, above about 200 EBC, add raisin, burnt sugar and dried fruit. Our guide to crystal and caramel malts explains how they are made.

Here is the catch. A good part of what crystal malt contributes does not ferment, which is why it adds sweetness and body. Use too much and the beer turns cloying and heavy. Most amber ales use roughly 8 to 15% crystal malt in total. Beyond that, the beer drinks sweet rather than rich.

For an original gravity of about 1.054 and around 5.3% ABV:

  • Pale ale malt: 4.15 kg (83%)
  • Munich malt: 0.35 kg (7%)
  • Crystal malt, around 120 EBC: 0.4 kg (8%)
  • Chocolate malt: 0.1 kg (2%), for a reddish hue and depth
  • Hops: about 30 to 35 IBU. Use a clean bittering hop at 60 minutes, then Cascade or Centennial at 10 minutes and at flameout.
  • Yeast: a clean American ale yeast

Mash at 66 to 67 °C. A hotter mash adds even more body on top of the crystal, which can tip the beer into heaviness.

An amber ale is a balancing act. The crystal malt brings sweetness and caramel. The hops bring bitterness and aroma to keep it from tasting sugary. Many homebrewed ambers taste flat because they have plenty of caramel but not enough bitterness to cut it.

A useful check is the ratio of bitterness to gravity. Divide the IBU by the gravity points. For 30 IBU at 1.054, that is 30 / 54, about 0.55, which tastes balanced to slightly bitter. Below about 0.4, an amber tends to taste sweet. Above about 0.8, it is heading towards IPA territory.

Ferment at 18 to 20 °C. A clean fermentation lets the caramel and hops show. Warm, fruity fermentation muddies the flavours. Bottle with about 2.3 to 2.5 volumes of CO2.

Crystal malt picks up moisture quickly in humid weather and goes stale and soft. Buy it in small amounts, keep it sealed and use it within a few months. A crystal malt that has absorbed moisture tastes flat and papery. That shows in a beer that depends on it.

Water is easier. Moderately hard water, the kind many Indian borewells give, suits an amber better than it suits a pale lager, because the darker malts lower the mash pH. If your water is very hard, a blend of half RO and half tap water is a sensible start. Aim for a little more chloride than you would in an IPA if you want the malt to feel rounder. Use a little more sulphate if you want the hops to bite.

Pour it and look first. It should be a clear copper with a hint of red. Then taste. Sweet and heavy: cut the crystal or mash cooler. Thin and bland: add a little more crystal or Munich. Harsh bitterness: balance with a touch more malt or move some hops later.

Change one variable at a time, taste carefully and write the result in your brew log. Over three or four batches that is how you learn to tune a beer to your own taste.
faqs: How much crystal malt should an amber ale have?
Roughly 8 to 15% of the grist in total. Above that the beer usually starts to taste sweet and heavy.
What is the difference between amber and red ale?
They overlap a great deal. Red ales tend to have a redder colour, often from a little roasted malt, while amber ales lean more on caramel.
Why does my amber ale taste too sweet?
Too much crystal malt, too hot a mash or not enough bitterness. Cut the crystal a little and check the bitterness to gravity balance.
Does the brand of crystal malt matter?
Colour and freshness matter more than the brand. Check the colour rating in EBC or Lovibond on the bag, buy what you can get fresh and keep it sealed against humidity.
